Thinking about a European festive city break this Christmas and New Year? The latest research from TUI Musement has revealed the destinations travellers are searching for the most, with London, Paris and Edinburgh leading the way.

Europe’s most popular cities for Christmas and New Year getaways have been revealed, with London emerging as the clear festive winner.

In its latest report, TUI Musement analysed Google searches for major European cities with populations of more than 150,000 people. Over the course of 12 months from November 2025 to October 2026, the tours and activities branch of TUI calculated the combined search volumes for “Christmas in [city]” and “New Year in [city]”.

According to the data, London has generated the most interest with a combined search volume of 272,320. Searches for “Christmas in London”, however, emerged as significantly more popular than during New Year at 184,100 and 88,200 searches, respectively.

"During the holiday season, the lights along Oxford Street and Regent Street, elaborately decorated storefronts and Winter Wonderland transform the city," TUI Musement said.

It also added that an iconic landmark like the Thames offers visitors river cruises with the perfect vantage point to see the city illuminated.

In second place comes the French capital Paris. The City of Love received a total of 252,800 Christmas and New Year’s related searches over the past year, which comes amid the run-up to the Champs-Élysées Christmas market revival.

After a decade-long absence, the Parisian holiday attraction now features 200 exhibitors housed in wooden chalets between the Rond-Point des Champs-Élysées and Place de la Concorde.

Rounding out the top three is another UK destination, Edinburgh, which received a combined search volume of 173,840. TUI Musement described its historic centre transforming "into a scene straight out of a Christmas story, with the traditional market at East Princes Street Gardens, fairground rides and festive storefront displays".

It also recommended Hogmanay – Scotland’s New Year's Eve and New Year celebrations – filled with concerts, street parties, torchlight processions and fireworks over Edinburgh Castle.

Fourth on the list with a combined search volume of 158,270, Vienna in Austria offers traditional Christmas markets, including on the Rathausplatz, which is the city's famous square in front of the town hall. In addition to classical music concerts held in historic venues, Vienna's Silvesterpfad New Year's Eve tradition, with a series of linked festivities across the city, is a must-go event.

In fifth is Strasbourg. Home to the oldest Christmas market in France, it reached 140,560 searches. Visitors can choose from eight markets spread across the historic centre, including the Christkindelsmärik, which was first held in 1570. "Another standout is the spectacular Christmas tree in Place Kléber, which stands approximately 100 feet tall," TUI Musement said.

Reaching a combined search volume of 139,630, and ranking sixth, is Amsterdam in the Netherlands. In 2026, the city's Light Festival marks 15 years since launching, where visitors will be able to enjoy art installations along the city's canal – either by boat or on foot. The festive atmosphere is completed by Christmas markets at the Museumplein public square and the ice-skating rink next to the Rijksmuseum of Dutch arts and history.

Italy’s capital, Rome, gained 126,750 searches. Coming in seventh place, holiday treats on offer include panettone and pandoro sweet breads, which are traditionally eaten during Christmas. When in Rome during the holiday season, browse the Christmas market at Piazza Navona. TUI Musement also recommended to visit the Nativity Scenes in St. Peter's Square at The Vatican.

Eighth on the list, Prague in Czechia gained 113,050 searches. With a climb up the Old Town Hall Tower, visitors get sweeping views of the Christmas market, Prague's rooftops and the large lit tree in the square.

While in Budapest, Hungary, which gained 110,510 searches, paying a visit to the Széchenyi Thermal Baths is a unique way to escape the winter chill after exploring the Christmas market at St. Stephen’s Basilica.

The top 10 is completed by Dublin, which gained 105,620 searches. The Irish capital is known for traditional Christmas lighting installation on Grafton Street and carol concerts at St. Patrick’s Cathedral.

Top 10 Christmas destinations

The most searched cities for travel during the Christmas and New Year holidays, according to the TUI Musement:

  • 1. London, UK: 272,320 searches
  • 2. Paris, France: 252,800 searches
  • 3. Edinburgh, UK: 173,840 searches
  • 4. Vienna, Austria: 158,270 searches
  • 5. Strasbourg, France: 140,560 searches
  • 6. Amsterdam, Netherlands: 139,630 searches
  • 7. Rome, Italy: 126,750 searches
  • 8. Prague, Czechia: 113,050 searches
  • 9. Budapest, Hungary: 110,510 searches
  • 10. Dublin, Ireland: 105,620 searches

Luxembourg's average full-time salary was more than five times Bulgaria's in 2025. Once local prices are taken into account, Greece ranks last, and Luxembourg's average salary buys about three times as much.

The average annual full-time adjusted salary in the EU was €41,464 in 2025, according to Eurostat figures published on 6 November 2026.

The gap between countries was wide. In Luxembourg, the average was more than five times as high as in Bulgaria.

To make pay easier to compare across countries, Eurostat expresses part-time salaries as full-time equivalents.

So, which countries had the highest and lowest average salaries? How do the rankings change when purchasing power is taken into account? And how do experts explain the differences?

Luxembourg pays the most

Across the 26 EU countries in Eurostat's ranking, average gross full-time adjusted salaries ranged from €16,201 in Bulgaria to €85,609 in Luxembourg, more than five times Bulgaria's figure.

Among the remaining countries, Denmark (€73,500), Ireland (€64,387), Belgium (€61,984) and Austria (€60,727) had the highest average salaries, rounding out the top five, all above €60,000.

Germany leads the 'Big Four'

Among the EU's 'Big Four' economies, Germany had the highest average salary at €56,360. France was just above the EU average at €44,734.

Gross full-time pay was much lower in the bloc's third- and fourth-largest economies, at €34,213 in Italy and €35,125 in Spain.

Other countries above the EU average included Finland (€50,960) and Sweden (€49,622).

At the bottom of the list, Bulgaria has the lowest average salary at €16,201. Greece (€18,772) and Hungary (€20,138) follow. Romania (€20,818), Slovakia (€21,661) and Latvia (€22,688) are also among the lowest.

These are gross salaries, and net earnings or incomes can vary because of differences in taxes and social contributions between countries.

The pay gap narrows once local prices are taken into account

The purchasing power standard (PPS) is a unit used to compare what money can buy across countries. It removes the effect of price differences across countries, so one PPS buys the same amount of goods and services everywhere.

The gap narrows when salaries are adjusted for differences in household prices, according to Euronews Business calculations using Eurostat data.

The highest average salary is about three times the lowest, compared with more than five times in euros.

Luxembourg still ranks first with 65,106 PPS. Bulgaria moves up two places to 24th, while Greece ranks last with 21,486 PPS.

The ranking also changes substantially. Slovenia moves above the EU average, while Sweden and the bloc's second-largest economy, France, fall below it.

Poland and Lithuania each rise three places. Austria moves from fifth to second place. Denmark falls from second to fourth, and Ireland from third to sixth.

Several Central and Eastern European countries move up in the PPS ranking. Romania climbs from 23rd to 18th place, the biggest rise at five places.

Estonia has the biggest drop, falling from 16th to 21st place.

Why do salaries differ so much?

According to experts, the main reasons are differences in economic development and productivity.

"By and large, of course, the main reason for the differences in wages across European countries is the different levels of economic development and productivity, and the output created by workers," Jaan Masso, associate professor in applied econometrics at the University of Tartu, told Euronews Business.

Štěpán Jurajda, professor at CERGE-EI in Prague, pointed to similar factors. "The main reasons for the large gaps in salaries across European countries include different endowments of physical and human capital (education) and different productivity (including institutions, effective regulation, R&D policies etc.)," he told Euronews Business.

Labour market rules also play a significant role. Masso said minimum wages and collective agreements affect how equal wages are. He noted that "typically wages are much more equal in the Scandinavian countries".

Why are prices higher in rich countries?

Jurajda explained that richer countries usually have higher prices. "A basic empirical fact is that as countries become richer, their price level rises," he said.

Masso gave an example from the services sector. In some services, productivity cannot rise much. "One still needs similar time to cut hair," he said. So in high-wage countries, higher labour costs lead to higher prices for services.

"Naturally, for people living in a particular country, the price-adjusted figure is more relevant," Masso added.

Jurajda urged caution when reading the rankings. "In general, small PPP-adjusted differences should not be interpreted as precise country rankings," he said.

Is the East-West gap closing?

Malte Lübker, a wage expert at the Institute of Economic and Social Research (WSI) at the Hans Böckler Foundation, said the gap has narrowed.

"In the past, employers in high-wage countries have often pointed at lower wages in Eastern Europe to call for domestic wage restraint. However, the gap has closed considerably over time," he told Euronews Business.

Lübker said that this also affects migration. "When you adjust for purchasing power, taking up a job in Germany is no longer such an attractive proposition for Polish workers," he said.

What do full-time salaries not show?

Adjusting salaries to full-time equivalents makes comparisons easier. But experts say it has limitations.

"Converting wage data into full-time equivalents is, of course, a useful statistical technique. However, we should not forget that full-time work might not be readily available," Lübker said.

"For others, primarily women, part-time employment is the only way to reconcile work and care responsibilities. This means that full-time wages are an imperfect proxy for living standards."

Masso noted that part-time work varies a lot across Europe. In many Eastern European countries, full-time work has been the norm, while in the Netherlands part-time work is very common.

Experts also point out that averages can hide large differences within a country. Masso said that in Luxembourg, "the high average might be affected by a smaller number of very highly paid jobs, e.g., in the financial sector".

Alongside his wife Carla Bruni, the ex-French president will face court in late 2027, accused of conspiracy and hiding witness tampering over alleged Libyan funding of his 2007 campaign.

Just six days before the appeal court is due to announce its decision in the case over the alleged Libyan financing of the 2007 presidential campaign, Nicolas Sarkozy already has another date with the courts.

Together with his wife, singer Carla Bruni, the former president is being sent for trial before the Paris criminal court in the case over the possibly paid-for retraction by Franco-Lebanese businessman Ziad Takieddine, a source close to the case said on Tuesday, 24 November.

All those placed under formal investigation in this case, including Mimi Marchand, "high priestess of the paparazzi," are being sent before the courts.

Nicolas Sarkozy and his partner will be tried for "criminal conspiracy to commit fraud as part of an organised gang" and "concealment of witness tampering".

Mimi Marchand will be tried for "witness tampering," "criminal conspiracy to commit fraud as part of an organised gang" and "with a view to preparing acts of corruption of foreign judicial personnel". Their trial is expected to take place from 3 November to 2 December 2027.

The defendants face a maximum sentence of ten years in prison and a fine of 150,000 euros.

The U-turns of Ziad Takieddine, key witness in the Libyan case

This new chapter in the former head of state's legal troubles is linked to the case that had earned him a five-year prison sentenceafter a guilty plea for criminal conspiracy. He had been released from prison after twenty days pending his appeal.

One of the main complainants in this case was Franco-Lebanese businessman Ziad Takieddine, who died in Lebanon last year. In 2016, he said he had helped deliver up to five million euros in cash from Libyan dictator Muammar Gaddafi to Nicolas Sarkozy and the former president's chief of staff in 2006 and 2007.

But in November 2020, Ziad Takieddine suddenly backtracked on his incriminating statements in an interview with French media before changing his mind once again.

This gave rise to allegations that Nicolas Sarkozy and his wife had called on "the queen of the paparazzi", Mimi Marchand, to pay this key witness to retract his statements, something they have always denied.

Carla Bruni is suspected in particular of having requested a clandestine phone line at the end of 2019 so she could communicate with Mimi Marchand about the Ziad Takieddine case.

Numerous run-ins with the law

In the case of the alleged financing of the 2007 presidential campaign, Nicolas Sarkozy became the first former French president to be jailed.

But the former occupant of the Élysée has also been definitively convicted in two other cases: the first linked to overspending during his unsuccessful 2012 election campaign, the second for later trying to obtain favours from a judge.

Mimi Marchand, for her part, was given an 18-month suspended prison sentence last year for blackmailing a television presenter, who feared she would publish images of her daughter leaving a police station.

A Swedish research team set out to identify who could benefit most from taking vitamin D supplements.

Low vitamin D in the summertime may be a bigger red flag for your health than in the winter months, a new study has found.

Vitamin D helps the body regulate calcium and phosphate in the body, keeping our bones, teeth and muscles healthy. Most of it comes from sunlight, while people can also get some vitamin D from foods such as oily fish, eggs and some mushrooms. Millions of Europeans also take vitamin D supplements, though randomised trials have largely failed to show that routine supplementation improves health or boosts longevity.

Researchers from Uppsala University in Sweden wondered if seasonal swings in vitamin D levels might help explain why. In Europe and much of the Northern Hemisphere, people build up stores of vitamin D in their fat during the sunny summer months, and they may draw on those reserves as their vitamin D levels naturally fall in the darker winter months.

“We need to better understand who truly needs vitamin D supplementation,” the researchers wrote.

To find out, the researchers analysed vitamin D levels in the blood of more than 12,000 older people in Sweden. They split participants into groups based on whether their blood was drawn in summer, from July to September, or in winter, from January to March.

People with low vitamin D levels in summer were more likely to fracture a bone or die over the next 11 years, on average, than those with high summer levels. Meanwhile, people who had low vitamin D levels in the winter months were not at increased risk of bone fracture or death, according to the study, which was published in the journal PLOS Medicine.

People were considered to have low vitamin D if their blood concentration was below 40 nanomoles per litre (nmo/L) and high levels if it was above 80 nmol/L.

The findings suggest summer could be the best time to test vitamin D levels. That could help doctors identify people who are chronically low and could benefit the most from supplements, the researchers said.

“We should think carefully about when we measure vitamin D,” the researchers wrote. “Winter measurements are heavily influenced by seasonal variation, whereas low vitamin D levels during summer are more likely to reflect persistently low vitamin D status and a higher risk of adverse health outcomes.”

This was an observational study, meaning it cannot show whether low vitamin D levels cause bone fractures or early death. It was also conducted mainly in white Swedish people, so the results may not directly apply to other groups. Still, the findings held even after the researchers accounted for age, sex, body size and other factors.

The researchers said more randomised trials are needed to identify the potential health benefits of supplements, ideally focused on people with low vitamin D levels in the summer.

Switzerland opened the office on 19 October, when Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis travelled to Pyongyang and met senior officials, including his counterpart Choe Son Hui.

North Korea has ordered Switzerland to shut its newly opened diplomatic office in Pyongyang and given its head 48 hours to leave the country in retaliation for Swiss sanctions on a children's camp linked to Russia.

State news agency KCNA reported on Wednesday that a senior Foreign Ministry official called in Astier Sylvain, who leads the Swiss mission, and handed him a written demand for the office's closure. Pyongyang declared him persona non grata.

The move follows a warning on Tuesday from Kim Yo Jong, the sister of leader Kim Jong Un and one of the regime's leading foreign policy voices, who called the sanctions an "open hostile act" that violated North Korean sovereignty.

The expulsion comes five weeks after Benn restarted operations in Pyongyang.

A rare Western channel under strain

Switzerland opened the office on 19 October, when Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis travelled to Pyongyang and met senior officials, including his counterpart Choe Son Hui.

KCNA said the talks covered "promoting dialogue and cooperation." The office reports to the Swiss embassy in Beijing, and Bern said it would help build direct contact with North Korean officials.

Switzerland has had diplomatic relations with North Korea since 1974 and remains one of the few Western states to keep a line open. Its development agency ran a cooperation office in Pyongyang from 1997, focused largely on humanitarian work, until it closed in March 2020, when North Korea sealed its borders during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The Swiss Foreign Ministry said on Tuesday that it wanted to keep channels of dialogue open despite political differences.

It stressed that reopening the office is separate from its sanctions policy, whether UN measures tied to North Korea's nuclear programme or the EU sanctions Switzerland has adopted over Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

The camp at the centre of the dispute

Bern recently added the Songdowon International Children's Camp, in the coastal city of Wonsan, to its sanctions list over Russia's war in Ukraine.

Swiss authorities say the facility is part of programmes that bring Ukrainian children from Russian-occupied territory to North Korea, where they are exposed to pro-Russian propaganda.

The UK sanctioned the camp in May, and the EU followed in September, freezing its assets and banning financial dealings with it. Given North Korea's minimal financial links with Europe, the practical effect of these measures is uncertain.

Kim Yo Jong said the camp serves "legitimate" cooperation between Pyongyang and Moscow. She did not directly respond to Western allegations that abducted Ukrainian children have been sent there for re-education.

North Korea has moved steadily closer to Russia during the war, supplying thousands of troops and large quantities of weapons to support Vladimir Putin's invasion, possibly in return for aid and military technology.

Closer relations with Moscow and Beijing have underpinned Kim Jong Un's more assertive foreign policy as he seeks to end the country's isolation and present it as part of a bloc opposed to Washington.
